paragraphs: A review of the principal objections that have been raised against the proposed court for the trial of impeachments will quite possibly uproot whatever remnants of unfavorable impressions may still linger on this subject.

The FIRST of these objections is that the provision in question mixes legislative and judicial authority in the same body, in violation of the important and well-established maxim that requires a separation between the different departments of power. The true meaning of this maxim has been discussed and settled elsewhere, and was shown to be entirely compatible with a partial intermixture of those departments for special purposes, so long as they are kept, in the main, distinct and unconnected. This partial intermixture is even, in some cases, not only proper but necessary for the mutual defense of the separate members of the government against each other. The ablest masters of political science admit that an absolute or qualified veto by the executive on the acts of the legislative body is an indispensable barrier against the legislature's encroachments on the executive. It may perhaps be argued with no less reason that the powers relating to impeachments are, as I suggested before, an essential check in the legislature's hands against the encroachments of the executive. These powers are divided between the two branches of the legislature, one given the right of accusing and the other the right of judging. This division avoids the problem of making the same persons both accusers and judges, and it guards against the danger of persecution from a factional spirit prevailing in either branch. Since two thirds of the Senate will be required for a conviction, the security this adds for innocence will be as complete as innocence itself could desire.

It is curious to see how vehemently this part of the plan is attacked, on the principle just noted, by men who profess to admire without exception the constitution of this State. That constitution makes the Senate, together with the chancellor and the judges of the Supreme Court, not only a court of impeachments but the highest court in the State in all cases, civil and criminal. The chancellor and judges are so few in number compared with the senators that the final judicial authority of New York may truly be said to reside in its Senate. If the Convention's plan is chargeable in this respect with a departure from the celebrated maxim that has been so often mentioned and seems to be so little understood, how much more blameworthy must the constitution of New York be?(1)

A SECOND objection to the Senate as a court of impeachments is that it contributes to an undue accumulation of power in that body, tending to give the government too aristocratic an appearance. The Senate, it is observed, is to have concurrent authority with the Executive in making treaties and in appointing to offices. If, say the objectors, the power of deciding all cases of impeachment is added to these prerogatives, it will give senatorial influence a decided predominance. To an objection so imprecise in itself, it is not easy to give a very precise answer. Where is the measure or standard to which we can appeal in deciding what will give the Senate too much influence, too little, or barely the proper amount? Would it not be both safer and simpler to dismiss such vague and uncertain calculations, to examine each power by itself, and to decide on general principles where it may be placed with the most advantage and the least inconvenience?

If we take this course, it will lead to a more intelligible, if not a more certain, result. The arrangement of the power of making treaties adopted in the Convention's plan will then, if I am not mistaken, appear fully justified by the considerations stated in a former number and by others that will come up under the next head of our inquiries. The expediency of joining the Senate with the Executive in the power of appointing to offices will, I trust, be shown in an equally satisfactory light in the discussions under that same head. And I flatter myself that the observations in my last paper must have gone a considerable way toward proving that it was not easy, if possible, to find a more fitting place for the power of deciding impeachments than the one that has been chosen. If this is truly the case, the hypothetical dread of too great a weight in the Senate ought to be dropped from our reasoning.

But this hypothesis, such as it is, has already been refuted in the remarks on the length of office prescribed for senators. There it was shown, both from historical examples and from the reason of the thing, that the most POPULAR branch of every government that has a republican character, because it is generally the favorite of the people, will be as generally a full match, if not an overmatch, for every other part of the government.

But apart from this most active and effective principle for securing the balance of the national House of Representatives, the Convention's plan has provided in its favor several important counterweights to the additional powers to be conferred on the Senate. The exclusive privilege of originating money bills will belong to the House of Representatives. The same house will have the sole right of bringing impeachments. Is this not a complete counterbalance to the Senate's right to decide them? The same house will be the umpire in all elections of the President that do not unite the votes of a majority of the whole number of electors, a case that, it cannot be doubted, will sometimes, if not often, occur. The constant possibility of this must be a rich source of influence for that body. The more it is considered, the more important this ultimate though contingent power will appear: that of deciding the competition among the most illustrious citizens of the Union for the first office in it. It would perhaps not be rash to predict that as a means of influence it will prove to outweigh all the peculiar powers of the Senate.

A THIRD objection to the Senate as a court of impeachments is drawn from the part it will have in appointments to office. It is imagined that the senators would be too lenient as judges of the conduct of men in whose official creation they had taken part. The principle of this objection would condemn a practice found in all the State governments, if not in all the governments we know of: that of making those who hold office during pleasure depend on the pleasure of those who appoint them. With equal plausibility it might be alleged in this case that the favoritism of the appointers would always be a refuge for the misbehavior of the appointed. But that practice, in contradiction to this principle, rests on a presumption. Those who appoint are responsible for the fitness and competence of the persons they choose, and they have an interest in a respectable and prosperous administration of affairs. The presumption is that these motives will give them enough disposition to remove from a share in the administration all those who by their conduct have proved themselves unworthy of the confidence placed in them. Facts may not always match this presumption. But if it is in the main just, it must destroy the supposition that the Senate, which will merely approve the choice of the Executive, would feel a bias toward the objects of that choice strong enough to blind its members to evidence of guilt so extraordinary as to have led the representatives of the nation to become the accusers.

If any further arguments were needed to show how unlikely such a bias is, they might be found in the nature of the Senate's part in appointments. It will be the office of the President to NOMINATE and, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to APPOINT. There will, of course, be no exercise of CHOICE on the part of the Senate. The senators may defeat one choice of the Executive and oblige him to make another, but they cannot themselves CHOOSE; they can only approve or reject the President's choice. They might even prefer some other person at the very moment they were assenting to the one proposed, because there might be no positive ground for opposing him. And if they withheld their assent, they could not be sure that the next nomination would fall on their own favorite, or on any other person they judged more deserving than the one rejected. Thus it could hardly happen that a majority of the Senate would feel any warmth toward the object of an appointment beyond what the appearance of merit might inspire and proofs of its absence would destroy.

A FOURTH objection to the Senate in the capacity of a court of impeachments is derived from its union with the Executive in the power of making treaties. This, it has been said, would make the senators their own judges in every case of a corrupt or treacherous exercise of that trust. After joining with the Executive in betraying the interests of the nation in a ruinous treaty, what prospect would there be, it is asked, of making them suffer the punishment they would deserve, when they were themselves to decide on the accusation brought against them for the treachery they had committed?

This objection has been spread with more zeal, and with a better appearance of reason, than any other raised against this part of the plan. And yet unless I am deceived, it rests on a mistaken foundation.

The security the Constitution essentially intends against corruption and treachery in making treaties is to be sought in the numbers and characters of those who are to make them. The JOINT AGENCY of the Chief Magistrate of the Union and of two thirds of the members of a body selected by the collective wisdom of the legislatures of the individual States is designed to be the pledge for the fidelity of the national councils in this matter. The Convention might properly have intended the punishment of the Executive for departing from the instructions of the Senate, or for lack of integrity in conducting the negotiations entrusted to him. It might also have had in view the punishment of a few leading individuals in the Senate who had prostituted their influence in that body as the mercenary instruments of foreign corruption. But it could not, with more or even equal propriety, have contemplated the impeachment and punishment of two thirds of the Senate for consenting to an improper treaty, any more than of a majority of that branch or of the other branch of the national legislature for consenting to a harmful or unconstitutional law. That is a principle which, I believe, has never been admitted into any government. How, in fact, could a majority in the House of Representatives impeach themselves? Not better, it is evident, than two thirds of the Senate could try themselves. And yet what reason is there that a majority of the House of Representatives, sacrificing the interests of society by an unjust and tyrannical act of legislation, should escape with impunity any more than two thirds of the Senate, sacrificing the same interests in an injurious treaty with a foreign power? The truth is that in all such cases it is essential to the freedom and the necessary independence of the body's deliberations that its members be exempt from punishment for acts done in a collective capacity. The security of society must depend on the care taken to place the trust in proper hands, to make it their interest to execute it faithfully, and to make it as difficult as possible for them to combine in any interest opposed to the public good.

As far as the misbehavior of the Executive is concerned, in perverting the instructions or going against the views of the Senate, we need not fear that the Senate will lack the disposition to punish the abuse of its confidence or to vindicate its own authority. We may count this far on its pride, if not on its virtue. And as far as the corruption of leading members is concerned, by whose arts and influence the majority may have been tricked into measures odious to the community, the usual tendency of human nature warrants the conclusion that, if the proofs of that corruption were satisfactory, the body would commonly show no lack of inclination to turn public resentment away from itself by readily sacrificing the authors of its mismanagement and disgrace.

1. In that of New Jersey, also, the final judicial authority is in a branch of the legislature. In New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania and South Carolina, one branch of the legislature is the court for the trial of impeachments.
